about: Interview questions and candidate answers written for OpenMeet's benchmarks (synthetic, no real person). Used for the follow-up check (bench_followups.py), spoken by Windows text-to-speech for the pipeline and room benchmarks (make_speech.ps1).

pairs.question: How would you design a rate limiter for a public API?
pairs.answer: I would start with a token bucket per API key, stored in Redis so every gateway node sees the same counts. Each request takes a token, and tokens refill at the plan's rate. We used that at my last job for our partner API, and it handled around two thousand requests a second. If a client runs out we return a 429 with a retry-after header, so well-behaved clients back off.

pairs.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.
pairs.answer: My manager wanted to ship a feature before the end of the quarter, and I thought the database migration behind it was too risky. I wrote up the failure cases and suggested we split the release, shipping the read path first. We argued about it for a week, but in the end she agreed, and the second half shipped two weeks later without an incident.

pairs.question: Walk me through how you would debug a memory leak in a production service.
pairs.answer: First I would confirm it is really a leak, so I would look at the memory graph over a few days and see whether it grows without levelling off. Then I would take two heap dumps a few hours apart and compare which object types grow. Last time that pointed at a cache that never evicted entries, keyed by user session. We added a size limit and the growth stopped.

pairs.question: Why did you choose Postgres over MongoDB for that project?
pairs.answer: Mostly because the data was relational. Orders, customers and invoices all referenced each other, and we needed transactions across them. The team also knew SQL well. MongoDB would have made the early prototypes faster, but we would have ended up rebuilding joins in application code.

pairs.question: What was the hardest technical problem you solved last year?
pairs.answer: Um, probably the search latency work. Our product search was taking about eight hundred milliseconds at the ninety fifth percentile. I profiled it and found most of the time went into re-ranking on the application server. I moved the first ranking stage into Elasticsearch with a function score query, and we got it down to about two hundred milliseconds.

pairs.question: Can you explain what eventual consistency means?
pairs.answer: It means that if no new writes happen, all the replicas will eventually return the same value, but for a while after a write different replicas can give different answers. You accept that to get availability and lower latency, for example in a shopping cart where a stale read for a second is fine.

pairs.question: How do you handle a teammate who keeps missing deadlines?
pairs.answer: I would talk to them one to one first, because there is usually a reason, like unclear requirements or too many parallel tasks. In one case the person was quietly covering on-call for another team. We raised it with the lead and moved the on-call duty, and their work got back on track.

pairs.question: How do you decide what to cover with unit tests versus integration tests?
pairs.answer: Pure logic like pricing rules or parsers gets unit tests, because they are fast and pin down edge cases. Anything that crosses a boundary, the database, a queue or another service, gets a smaller number of integration tests against real dependencies in containers. I try to keep the integration suite under ten minutes so people actually run it.

pairs.question: How would you make a file upload service resilient to failures?
pairs.answer: I would upload in chunks with resumable sessions, so a dropped connection only loses one chunk. The chunks go straight to object storage with presigned URLs, and a small metadata service records which chunks arrived. When all of them are there, a background worker assembles and checks the file.

pairs.question: What did you personally contribute to the payments migration?
pairs.answer: We moved from a homegrown billing system to Stripe. We planned it over two months, we ran both systems in parallel, and we compared every invoice. We found a few rounding differences and fixed them before the switch.

pairs.question: Have you worked with Kubernetes?
pairs.answer: Yes, a little, mainly deploying services with Helm charts.

pairs.question: How would you evaluate a model that flags fraudulent transactions?
pairs.answer: Accuracy is useless there because fraud is rare, so I would look at precision and recall at the operating threshold, and the cost of each kind of mistake. A false positive annoys a real customer and a false negative loses money. I would also check the results per segment, like new versus old accounts, and watch for drift after launch.
